Let $\pi$ be a prior probability on $(E,\mathcal S)$ and let $Q:E\to T$ be a probability kernel dominated by a sigma-finite measure $\nu$ on $(T,\mathcal T)$, with specified nonnegative jointly measurable density $\ell:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$:
$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces. Suppose $\Pi$ is a supplied probability kernel from $\mathsf Y$ to $\Theta$; write its probability measure at $y$ as $\Pi_y$. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel from $\Theta$ to a measurable future-observation space $(\mathsf Z,\mathcal Z)$. Define the **posterior-predictive probability kernel** by
$$Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(B):=\int_\Theta Q_\theta(B)\,\Pi_y(d\theta),\qquad y\in\mathsf Y,\ B\in\mathcal Z.$$
A probability kernel has pointwise probability-measure sections and measurable event evaluations, as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. This definition takes the posterior kernel as supplied; it does not form a likelihood quotient.

For a proper-prior dominated model, [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] supplies one such data-indexed kernel when the sampling laws have a specified nonnegative jointly measurable density against a sigma-finite data measure. Its stated filler on zero or infinite normalizers is part of that kernel version.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

derivations.claim: Fix $y\in\mathsf Y$ and regard $\Pi_y$ as a probability measure on $\Theta$. By [F2], $Q$ is a probability kernel, so [F3] gives a joint probability measure $J_y$ on $\Theta\times\mathsf Z$ satisfying $J_y(A\times B)=\int_A Q_\theta(B)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)$ and the iterated-integral identity for every nonnegative product-measurable function. Taking $A=\Theta$ shows $Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(B)=J_y(\Theta\times B)$; hence it is the second marginal of a probability measure and is itself a probability measure. The same identity applied to $(\theta,z)\mapsto g(z)$ gives the displayed integral formula.

Fix $B\in\mathcal Z$. The function $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta(B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable by [F2], so $(y,\theta)\mapsto Q_\theta(B)$ is $\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T$-measurable as the composition with the measurable coordinate projection. By [F4], $y\mapsto\int_\Theta Q_\theta(B)\Pi_y(d\theta)$ is measurable. By [F1] this is $Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(B)$, proving kernel measurability.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is

- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is

probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: Let $s_2(\theta)=\int z^2Q_\theta(dz)$. It is measurable by [F4]. Since $\int s_2\,d\Pi_y<\infty$, the set $E_y=\{s_2<\infty\}$ is measurable and has $\Pi_y(E_y)=1$. On $E_y$, $|z|\le 1+z^2$ gives a finite first absolute moment, so $\mu(\theta)$ is finite and measurable by [F4]. Expanding the square in the variance definition [F3] gives $v(\theta)=s_2(\theta)-\mu(\theta)^2\ge0$, hence $\mu(\theta)^2\le s_2(\theta)$; therefore $\mu$ is square-integrable under $\Pi_y$ and $v$ is integrable.

For the joint-model hypotheses in the Statement, let $B$ be a measurable future event and $G\in\mathcal G$. The function $\theta\mapsto Q_\theta(B)$ is measurable by [F9]. Apply [F5] to the posterior conditional law and this bounded function to obtain $\int_G Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y(B)\,dP=\int_G Q_X(B)\,dP$. Since $G\in\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H$, apply [F5] again to the conditional law $Q_X$ to get $\int_G Q_X(B)\,dP=P(G\cap\{Z\in B\})$. By [F2], the mixture has probability-measure sections and measurable evaluations; these event identities therefore make $Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y$ a regular conditional distribution of $Z$ given $\mathcal G$ under [F6].

By [F1], $Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}$ is the mixture defined from $Q_\theta$ and $\Pi_y$. Apply [F2] to $g(z)=z^2$ to obtain $\int z^2Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(dz)=\int s_2\,d\Pi_y<\infty$. Apply [F2] to $|z|$ and use $|z|\le1+z^2$ to see that $Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}$ has finite first absolute moment. Applying [F2] to the nonnegative positive and negative parts of $z$ and subtracting their finite integrals gives $\int zQ_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(dz)=\int\mu\,d\Pi_y$.

Apply [F5] to $z$ and $z^2$ under $Q_X$. Writing $m:=\mu(X)$ and $s:=s_2(X)$, their conditional-integration identities give $\mathbb E[1_A Z]=\mathbb E[1_A m]$ and $\mathbb E[1_A Z^2]=\mathbb E[1_A s]$ for every $A\in\mathcal H$, and $\mathbb E[s]=\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$. Applying [F5] to $s_2$ under $\Pi_Y$ gives a conditional version of $s$ with expectation $\mathbb E[s]$; hence $D:=\{y:\int s_2(\theta)\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty\}$ has full probability. Take the zero-filled representative $\bar s(Y):=\int s_2(\theta)\Pi_y(d\theta)$ on $D$ and zero elsewhere. Then $\mathbb E[\bar s(Y)]=\mathbb E[s]=\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$ and $\Pi_Y(E)=1$ almost surely for $E=\{\theta:s_2(\theta)<\infty\}$. The conditioning identity for $X$ then gives $P(X\in E)=1$. By step 1.1, $m^2\le s$ and $0\le v(X)\le s$ almost surely; hence $m\in L^2$ and $v(X)$ is integrable, with $v(X)=s-m^2$ almost surely. Because $X$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable and these moment functions are measurable, $m,s,v(X)$ are $\mathcal H$-measurable. The first event identity extends from bounded simple $\mathcal H$-measurable multipliers to $1_A m$ by simple approximation and truncation; $2|mZ|\le m^2+Z^2$ and $m^2\in L^1$ justify the limits. Thus $\mathbb E[1_A mZ]=\mathbb E[1_A m^2]$, and expansion gives $\mathbb E[1_A(Z-m)^2]=\mathbb E[1_A(s-m^2)]=\mathbb E[1_Av(X)]$ for every $A\in\mathcal H$. This proves eventwise that $m$ is the conditional-mean version of $Z$ and $v(X)$ is the conditional-variance version given $\mathcal H$.

On $E_y$, $s_2=v+\mu^2$, and off $E_y$ the set is $\Pi_y$-null. By [F3] and step 2.1, $\operatorname{Var}_{Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}}(Z)=\int s_2\,d\Pi_y-(\int\mu\,d\Pi_y)^2=\int v\,d\Pi_y+\int\mu^2\,d\Pi_y-(\int\mu\,d\Pi_y)^2=\int v\,d\Pi_y+\operatorname{Var}_{\Pi_y}(\mu)$. This proves both displayed kernel identities without choosing conditional-expectation representatives.

On the full-measure data domain where $b(Y):=\int s_2\,d\Pi_Y<\infty$, set $c(Y):=\int\mu\,d\Pi_Y$, $d(Y):=\int\mu^2\,d\Pi_Y$, and $e(Y):=\int v\,d\Pi_Y$, and extend $b,c,d,e$ by zero on its null complement, using the signed zero-filled extension for $c$. By [F5] and the kernel identities in steps 2.1 and 3.1, $c,b$ are conditional first- and second-moment versions of $Z$ given $\mathcal G$, while $c,d,e$ are conditional moments of $m,m^2,v(X)$ given $\mathcal G$. Since $Y$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, these functions of $Y$ are $\mathcal G$-measurable. Also $\mathbb E[b(Y)]=\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$, $c^2\le b$ almost surely since $b-c^2=\operatorname{Var}_{Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y}(Z)\ge0$, and $d\le b<\infty$ almost surely since $\mu^2\le s_2$.

For each $A\in\mathcal G$, the same simple-multiplier and truncation argument as in step 2.2, now applied to $m$ with center $c(Y)$ and to $Z$ with that same center, gives $\mathbb E[1_A(m-c(Y))^2]=\mathbb E[1_A(d-c(Y)^2)]$ and $\mathbb E[1_A(Z-c(Y))^2]=\mathbb E[1_A(b(Y)-c(Y)^2)]$; the bounds $2|c m|\le c^2+m^2$ and $2|cZ|\le c^2+Z^2$ justify the respective truncations. Thus $d-c^2$ and $b-c^2$ are the conditional-variance versions of $m$ and $Z$ given $\mathcal G$. The kernel identity in step 3.1 gives $b-c^2=e+(d-c^2)$, so the conditional variance of $Z$ given $\mathcal G$ is the expected conditional variance given $\mathcal H$ plus the conditional variance of the conditional mean. These event-identity versions are choice-free; under [A1] they may also be read as conditional-expectation equivalence classes by [F5], while [F8] gives the eventwise version convention. No value on a null data fiber is thereby made canonical.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

$$\ell \text{ is an infimum of } S \iff \big[(\forall s \in S)\, \ell \le s\big] \text{ and } \big[(\forall \ell' \in \mathbb{R})\, \big((\forall s \in S)\, \ell' \le s\big) \Rightarrow \ell' \le \ell\big].$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$

$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.

$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

supplier_interfaces.excerpt:
Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(B):=\int_\Theta Q_\theta(B)\,\Pi_y(d\theta),\qquad y\in\mathsf Y,\ B\in\mathcal Z.$$
A probability kernel has pointwise probability-measure sections and measurable event evaluations, as in [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. This definition takes the posterior kernel as supplied; it does not form a likelihood quotient.

For a proper-prior dominated model, [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] supplies one such data-indexed kernel when the sampling laws have a specified nonnegative jointly measurable density against a sigma-finite data measure. Its stated filler on zero or infinite normalizers is part of that kernel version.

Let $\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability measure on $\Theta$ and $Q_\theta$ a future probability kernel on $\mathbb R$. Put
$$s_2(\theta)=\int_{\mathbb R}z^2\,Q_\theta(dz),$$and assume $\int_\Theta s_2(\theta)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty$. On the full-measure set $E_y=\{\theta:s_2(\theta)<\infty\}$, define$$\mu(\theta)=\int z\,Q_\theta(dz),\qquad v(\theta)=\operatorname{Var}_{Q_\theta}(Z),$$and set $\mu=v=0$ off $E_y$ when integrating them against $\Pi_y$. Then$$\int z\,Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}(dz)=\int\mu(\theta)\,\Pi_y(d\theta),$$
$$\operatorname{Var}_{Q_y^{\mathrm{pred}}}(Z)=\int v(\theta)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)+\operatorname{Var}_{\Pi_y}(\mu).$$
These kernel identities are choice-free. For the conditional interpretation, suppose a joint probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ carries measurable random elements $Y$ (data), $X$ (parameter), and $Z$ (future observation). Let $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F$ be sub-sigma-algebras such that $Y$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable and $X$ is $\mathcal H$-measurable. Assume $\Pi_{Y}$ is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ and $Q_X$ is a regular conditional distribution of $Z$ given $\mathcal H$. Thus the future law given the information in $\mathcal H$ is assumed to depend on it through $X$ alone. If $\mathbb E[Z^2]<\infty$, then $Q^{\mathrm{pred}}_Y$ is a regular conditional distribution of $Z$ given $\mathcal G$, and the displayed identities give the corresponding conditional-mean and conditional-variance versions almost surely. Here conditional variance means a version of the conditional expectation of the squared deviation from the corresponding conditional-mean version, using [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. Identifying those versions with conditional-expectation equivalence classes uses AC, as stated below. Values on null data fibers remain version-dependent.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $Q^{\mathrm{pred}}(\{1\})=\frac12Q_0(\{1\})+\frac12Q_1(\{1\})=\frac12(0)+\frac12(1)=\frac12$. Since its support is $\{0,1\}$, this is $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)$, with mean $1/2$ and variance $1/4$.
The conditional means are $\mu(0)=0$ and $\mu(1)=1$, and both conditional variances are zero. Thus $\mathbb E_\Pi[\operatorname{Var}(Z\mid\theta)]=0$ and $\operatorname{Var}_\Pi(\mu)=1/4$.

The predictive variance in step 1.1 equals the sum of those two terms in step 1.2, as asserted by [F2]. Here the entire predictive variance comes from posterior uncertainty about $\theta$, while future sampling conditional on $\theta$ contributes zero.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ have a supplied posterior probability kernel $\Pi_y$, let $(\mathsf A,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable action space, and let $L:\Theta\times\mathsf A\to[0,\infty]$ be a measurable function on the product measurable space [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. This strengthens the section-measurability convention in [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] so that posterior integrals vary measurably with measurable action rules.

For a fixed data fiber $y$ and action $a$, define the **posterior risk** only when
$$\rho_y(a):=\int_\Theta L(\theta,a)\,\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty.$$
A **pointwise Bayes action** at $y$ is a finite-risk action attaining the minimum among all finite-risk actions. On a declared measurable data domain $D$, a **Bayes action rule** is a measurable map $\delta:D\to\mathsf A$ whose finite posterior risk attains that minimum at every $y\in D$. This definition makes no assertion that finite-risk actions or measurable minimizing rules always exist. It therefore does not infer a Bayes action merely from the existence of an infimum. The sampling risk in [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] is a different integral, taken over the data law at a fixed parameter.

Let $\Pi$ be a posterior probability kernel on a nonempty finite class $\Theta=\{1,\ldots,k\}$ with the sigma-algebra of all its subsets; give the action class the same measurable structure and use zero–one loss $L(\theta,a)=\mathbf 1_{\{\theta\ne a\}}$. Every posterior-mass maximizer minimizes pointwise posterior risk. The least-indexed posterior-mass maximizer is a measurable, finite-risk Bayes action rule. This statement is choice-free.

derivations.claim: Under zero–one loss, the risks are $1-\Pi(\{0\})=0.7$ for action $0$ and $1-\Pi(\{1\})=0.3$ for action $1$. Thus action $1$ is the unique zero–one Bayes action, in agreement with [F2].
Under the asymmetric loss, the risk of action $1$ is $3\Pi(\{0\})=0.9$, while the risk of action $0$ is $\Pi(\{1\})=0.7$. Both risks are finite and the lower one is attained uniquely by action $0$.

The two loss functions therefore select different actions under the same posterior: zero–one loss selects $1$, while the stated asymmetric loss selects $0$. This demonstrates that posterior modes alone do not determine a Bayes action without a specified loss.

For a probability measure $\Pi_y$ on $\mathbb R$, a **posterior median** is any $m\in\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$\Pi_y((-\infty,m])\ge \tfrac12\quad\text{and}\quad\Pi_y([m,\infty))\ge\tfrac12.$$
The two inequalities, rather than a density-based definition, apply to discrete, continuous, and mixed posteriors and permit more than one median.

Let $\Pi$ be a posterior probability kernel on $\mathbb R$ and take the action space to be $\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Let
$$D_1=\left\{y:\int_{\mathbb R}|\theta|\,\Pi_y(d\theta)<\infty\right\}.$$
Then $D_1$ is measurable. For every $y\in D_1$, every posterior median minimizes the finite absolute posterior risk $a\mapsto\int|\theta-a|\,\Pi_y(d\theta)$. The measurable lower-median rule from [[lem-lower-posterior-median-is-measurable]] is therefore an attained Bayes action rule on $D_1$.

derivations.claim: For $m\in[0,1]$, $\Pi((-\infty,m])\ge1/2$ and $\Pi([m,\infty))\ge1/2$, so [F1] makes every such $m$ a median.

For $m\in[0,1]$, $\rho(m)=\frac12|m|+\frac12|1-m|=\frac12$. For $a<0$, $\rho(a)=\frac12(-a)+\frac12(1-a)=\frac12-a>\frac12$; for $a>1$, $\rho(a)=\frac12a+\frac12(a-1)=a-\frac12>\frac12$. Thus precisely the interval $[0,1]$ minimizes risk, in agreement with [F2].

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be measurable spaces and let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel. For $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a set-valued rule $C$ is **graph-measurable** when
$$\{(y,\theta)\in\mathsf Y\times\Theta:\theta\in C(y)\}\in\mathcal Y\otimes\mathcal T.$$
It is a **posterior credible set at level $1-\alpha$** when it is graph-measurable and
$$\Pi_y(C(y))\ge 1-\alpha\qquad\text{for every }y\text{ in its declared data domain}.$$
The posterior-mass function is measurable by integration of the indicator of the membership graph against the kernel. If a density is available relative to a specified dominating measure, a highest-posterior-density region selects parameter values with largest density; such regions need not be intervals and may be disconnected or nonunique.

Let $\Pi_y$ be a posterior probability kernel on $\mathbb R$ and let $0<\alpha<1$. Define $C_\alpha(y)=[q_{\alpha/2}(y),q_{1-\alpha/2}(y)]$ using the quantiles from [[lem-measurable-posterior-quantile-and-cdf-bracketing]]. Then $C_\alpha$ is graph-measurable and $\Pi_y(C_\alpha(y))\ge1-\alpha$ for every $y$. Thus equal-tailed posterior quantile intervals are one kind of credible set.

derivations.claim: The joint density/mass is $1\cdot\theta$ at $Y=1$ and $1\cdot(1-\theta)$ at $Y=0$. Its marginal masses are $\int_0^1\theta d\theta=1/2$ and $\int_0^1(1-\theta)d\theta=1/2$. Therefore the posterior densities are $p(\theta\mid Y=1)=2\theta$ and $p(\theta\mid Y=0)=2(1-\theta)$; each conditional law integrates to one and satisfies the defining conditioning identity.

Their CDFs on $[0,1]$ are $F_1(x)=x^2$ and $F_0(x)=1-(1-x)^2$. Hence the central 95% intervals are $C(1)=[\sqrt{0.025},\sqrt{0.975}]$ and $C(0)=[1-\sqrt{0.975},1-\sqrt{0.025}]$. Each has posterior mass $0.975-0.025=0.95$, also in accordance with [F1, F2].

For fixed true $\theta_0=0.005$, $\sqrt{0.025}>0.005$ because $0.025>0.005^2$. Also $1-\sqrt{0.975}>0.005$ because $0.975<0.995^2$. Thus $\theta_0$ lies below the lower endpoint of both possible intervals, so $P_{\theta_0}\{\theta_0\in C(Y)\}=0$, not $0.95$. This verifies that posterior credibility is not a frequentist coverage guarantee.
